newsitem.title: RUSSIA: The top officials in the new Russian government.
newsitem.headline: The top officials in the new Russian government.

text.p: The following are brief profiles of the top officials in the Russian government unveiled on Monday by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
Appointed as first deputy prime ministers were:

ANATOLY CHUBAIS, 41, who moved 10 days ago from Kremlin chief-of-staff to first deputy prime minister. The father of Russia's massive post-communist privatisation programme, he is hailed by the West as the country's leading reformer and condemned by communists and their allies as a danger to Russia.

He is charged with overseeing the Russian economy and will also serve as finance minister. He was removed in January 1996 as first deputy premier in charge of economic reforms, but won back Yeltsin's trust by leading the president's come-from-behind re-election victory last year.

BORIS NEMTSOV, 37, telegenic governor of Nizhny Novgorod, if often dubbed the "golden boy" of Russia's market reforms. Under Nemtsov, the carmaking city and surrounding region pioneered privatisation and other market reforms and are seen by many Western experts as a model for the rest of Russia.
Nemtsov will handle social programmes, natural monopolies and deal with powerful regional authorities -- one of the most difficult portfolios in the new government.
Six men will serve as deputy prime ministers, two of whom retain their posts.

VLADIMIR BULGAK, 55, has been minister of communications since November 1991, a month before the collapse of the Soviet Union. A radio engineer by training, Moscow-native Bulgak spent his career as an official at Moscow Municipal Radio Broadcasting Network and then the Soviet Ministry of Communications.

Although he has often acted behind the scenes, he is outspoken in attempting to bar foreign investors from gaining too large a share in the telecommunications industry, which he says would threaten national security.

OLEG SYSUYEV, 42, mayor of Samara, one of Russia's largest cities known for its aerospace and defence industries. He started his career in the aerospace industry and then got involved in local politics in Samara, then called Kyibyshev, as a Communist Party official. He won re-election by a wide margin last fall and is considered to be a reformer.

ALFRED KOKH, 35, head of Russia's privatisation agency and ally of Chubais. Born in Kazakhstan, Kokh is an economist who trained and worked in St. Petersburg in an electronics factory before coming to Moscow as Chubais's deputy in 1993. From 1991 to 1993 he worked in the St. Petersburg privatisation committee.

YAKOV URINSON, 52, deputy economy minister until Monday, who has said that only further reform can bring economic recovery to Russia. He recently called for firms unable to pay their debts to sell off their property.

ANATOLY KULIKOV, 50, a career soldier known for conservative political views and tough talk on crime, was appointed deputy prime minister in February. He also retained his job as Interior Minister, which he has held since July 1995. Under his job description announced in February, he oversees tax police, customs and other agencies dealing with economic crime. His past calls to nationalise some commercial banks has raised some concern about his commitment to reform.

VALERY SEROV, 56, deputy prime minister in charge of cooperation with the Commonwealth of Independent States and regional politics, retains the position to which he was appointed in August. A construction engineer by training, he served in the 1980s as an official at the USSR State Planning Committee and State Construction Committee.
